sources.name: MedlinePlus: Blood Thinners
sources.text: What are blood thinners? Blood thinners are medicines that prevent blood clots from forming. They do not break up clots that you already have. But they can stop those clots from getting bigger. It's important to treat blood clots, because clots in your blood vessels and heart can cause heart attacks, strokes, and blockages. Who needs blood thinners? You may need a blood thinner if you have: Certain heart or blood vessel diseases An abnormal heart rhythm called atrial fibrillation A heart valve replacement A risk of blood clots after surgery Congenital heart defects What are the different types of blood thinners? There are different types of blood thinners: Anticoagulants, such as heparin or warfarin (also called Coumadin), slow down your body's process of making clots. Antiplatelets, such as aspirin and clopidogrel, prevent blood cells called platelets from clumping together to form a clot. Antiplatelets are mainly taken by people who have had a heart attack or stroke. How can I take blood thinners safely? When you take a blood thinner, follow the directions carefully. sources.name: Pharmacology for Nurses: Antiplatelets
sources.text: Antiplatelet drugs work by decreasing platelet activation and/or platelet adhesion. They are used for various indications including prevention and treatment of cardiovascular disease and prevention of ischemic stroke. P2Y12 Inhibitors P2Y12 inhibitors are potent antiplatelet agents that work as antagonists at the P2Y12 subunit of the ADP receptor on the platelet surface, which decreases platelet activation at the site of vessel injury. Because of their effect on bleeding, it is recommended that P2Y12 inhibitors be discontinued 5–7 days prior to surgery, depending on the agent. The advantage of cangrelor is that it inhibits platelets nearly immediately upon administration, and platelet function recovers within an hour of medication discontinuation. sources.name: Medical-Surgical Nursing: Thrombocytopenia
sources.text: 16.4 Thrombocytopenia Learning Objectives By the end of this section, you will be able to: Discuss the pathophysiology, risk factors, and clinical manifestations associated with thrombocytopenia Describe the diagnostics and laboratory values in thrombocytopenia Apply nursing concepts and plan associated nursing care for the patient with thrombocytopenia Evaluate the efficacy of nursing care for the patient with thrombocytopenia Describe the medical therapies for thrombocytopenia Low platelet count syndrome, or thrombocytopenia , is an uncommon hematologic condition characterized by decreased numbers of platelets (thrombocytes) in the bloodstream, affecting three out of 100,000 people yearly in the United States (NORD, 2022).
